## Aside: Some Technical Bits in the Loop-Based Solution

Look back in last lecture's [Class Activity: Voronoi Art](https://us.prairielearn.com/pl/course_instance/228149/assessment/2722853/) at `voronoi_loop_answer_nb.py`.

:::

::: {.column width=40%}
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 520" width="100%" >
  <rect x="8" y="8" width="784" height="504" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="8"/>
  <circle cx="180" cy="170" r="12" fill="#e74c3c" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="4"/>
  <circle cx="260" cy="330" r="12" fill="#2952ff" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="4"/>
  <circle cx="540" cy="210" r="12" fill="#8ee36f" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="4"/>
</svg>

Size of the image: $n$\
($n =$ width $\times$ height)

Density of centers: $d$

Number of centers: $dn$
:::

:::

::: notes
1. $O(n)$.
1. Hopefully $O(dn)$.
1. $O(dn^2)$.
1. $O(n)$.

Can we do better?  Do we need to "visit" (do something for) every pixel?  Yes: At a minimum we need to write out a colour for that pixel.  So, we probably can't avoid $O(n)$.  But what about the dependence on number of centers?  Can we avoid doing something for each pixel-center combination?
:::


## Can we do better?

![](/images/Valgorithmgrid.jpg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="A large grid with 3 colored centers."}

::: notes
- Starting at each center, fill in the immediate neighbours.
- Then fill in the neighbours of the neighbours.
- Repeat until all pixels are filled.
- Each pixel is visited just once.
- But how do we know which pixel to fill next?  
  - We want to fill all the 1-neighbours, then all the 2-neighbours, etc.
  - We know that the 1-neighbours are the neighbours of the centers.
  - We know that the 2-neighbours are the neighbours of the 1-neighbours.
  - Can we arrange to see the centers first, then their neighbours, then their neighbours, ...?
:::


## Data Structure: Queue

To implement the fill we use a datastructure called a *queue*.

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
![](/images/penguins.jpg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Penguins in a line jumping off an ice flow into the water."}
:::

::: {.column}
Operations on a queue:

- `enqueue(d)`: places data `d` at the "end" / "bottom" of the queue.
- `dequeue()`: removes and returns the element at the "start" / "top" of the queue.
:::

:::

::: notes
How does the queue differ from the stack you were exploring in the lab?  These two structures are also sometimes called FIFO (queue) or LIFO (stack).

A queue is a generic name for a data structure with this behaviour, and `enqueue` and `dequeue` are generic names for the operations that you perform on this data structure.

You will actually implement a queue in Python using the `deque` data structure from the `collections` module, and the methods for `enqueue` and `dequeue` will have different names.
:::


## Pattern: Flood Fill

::::: columns
::: {.column}
![](/images/FF1.png){fig-alt="Grid with each pixel numbered, pixel 63 highlighted blue, subset of pixels surrounded by a yellow curve."}
:::

::: {.column}
- enqueue a starting point
- while the queue is not empty:
   - v = dequeue
   - for each valid neighbor w of v:
      - process w
      - enqueue w
:::
::::::

## Designing a Solution

We’ll use [`collections.deque`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html#collections.deque) as our queue. 

1. What should we put on the queue?
1. What `deque` methods will we use?
1. How can we check if a `deque` is empty?
1. What are the  "neighbors" of pixel `(x,y)`?
1. What would be an _invalid_ neighbor?

Aside: Queues are also available from Python's [`queue` library](https://docs.python.org/3/library/queue.html).

::: notes
1. Centers to start, then neighbour pixels.  What do we need to know about the thing put on the queue?  Its location, maybe colour.
1. `append` and `popleft`.  Alternatively, could use `appendleft` and `pop`.  Pick a direction and stick with it!
1. Could check `len(queue) == 0`.  Or could use `while queue:` loop (remember that Python always has a boolean interpretation of any piece of data).
1. `(x-1,y)`, `(x,y-1)`, `(x+1,y)`, `(x,y+1)`.
1. Pixel outside an image or pixel that has already been processed.

Queue library features:
- Safe for parallel algorithms and in some cases more powerful (such as [`queue.PriorityQueue`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/queue.html#queue.PriorityQueue)).
- Slower and take up more memory. 
:::
